title: On Buddha-Recitation (Annotated Sayings of Master Chewu)
author: Compiled and annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: A single recitation of the Buddha’s name, free of all other conditions; when the ten recitations are perfected, one instantly transcends many kalpas.

inline.s: Course
Textbook
Master Chewu
Sayings
A single recitation of the Buddha’s name, free of all other conditions; when the ten recitations are perfected, one instantly transcends many kalpas.
But so long as thought succeeds thought without interruption, the subduing, the severing, the cultivating, and the realising that result cannot be conceived or spoken of.
Master Yinguang said:
“The Sayings of Chewu are indeed
(in truth)
the most essential instruction of the Pure Land school.”
(From the Preface to the Collected Works of Chan Master Mengdong)

This book is the standard and the guide for Buddha-recitation, a jewel among treatises, and so it is named “On Buddha-Recitation.” The words within it are the very practice of Master Chewu. Not only did the master speak them, he also accomplished them, and confirmed them through the many auspicious signs of his rebirth — which is the most rare and admirable aspect of all.

“To know the way through the mountain, one must ask one who has already travelled it.” Master Chewu knew the time of his passing ten months before he died, and the auspicious signs of his rebirth appeared in abundance; thus he is one who has already traversed the road to the Land of Bliss. His words are true and his meaning is real, and to act in accordance with them can never go wrong.

[gui nie] refers to the gnomon (gui biao), a metaphor for a standard or a rule. [Gnomon] an astronomical instrument of ancient China: a ruler (gui) is laid flat on a stone base with a pole (biao) set up at each of the north and south ends. From the length of the sun’s shadow one can determine the solar terms and the length of the year.

Although “On Buddha-Recitation” comprises only thirty-nine sections and few in words, yet concerning the principle, practice, conduct, and realisation of the Pure Land school it gives a penetrating and comprehensive exposition, and it instructs one to understand the First Principle and to work upon the mind-ground — truly a guide of study and practice for all who recite the Buddha’s name. Therefore one should earnestly embrace it with all one’s heart, set it before one’s seat, and read it, awaken to it, and practise it constantly, so that all may enter deeply into the realm of the Pure Land teaching and ascend directly to the highest lotus seat, in order not to be unworthy of the master’s great compassionate heart.
[The First Principle] the supreme and unsurpassed truth, which is the reality of all dharmas. The Buddha said:

“All dharmas are false and illusory; in the very place where they cease, that is called real, that is called reality, that is called the dharma-realm, that is called ultimate wisdom, that is called the truth of the First Principle, that is called the emptiness of the First Principle.”
(The Mahaparinirvana Sutra,
Fascicle Forty,
the Kaundinya Chapter.) [The reality of all dharmas] what is called “reality” is the true state of things; “the reality of all dharmas” is the true state of all dharmas. In the Buddha-store Sutra,
the Buddha-Recitation Chapter, the second, the Buddha said:
“What is called the reality of all dharmas? That is, all dharmas are ultimately empty, without any existence.”
The Diamond Sutra says:
“Whatever has form is false and illusory.”
[quan quan fu ying] to hold fast earnestly and never forget. Quan quan: to grasp tightly and not let go, extended to mean earnest and sincere; fu ying: to keep deeply in the mind.

Of the thirty-nine sections in the whole work, the first thirty-eight are from the “Dharma Words” portion of the Collected Works of Master Chewu, while the last section is excerpted from the Collected Works of Master Chewu, “Reply to the Layman Xiangyan.” The numbering and titles of the sections were added by the annotator for ease of understanding and reference, and are not part of the original text.

blocks.text: A Brief Biography of the Master

inline.s: Master Chewu (
), an eminent monk of the Qing dynasty, a native of Fengrun in Hebei. His lay surname was Ma, his given name Jixing, and his style name Chewu,
his sobriquet Mengdong, and he lived in the Qianlong era. He was the

thirty-sixth patriarch of the Linji school and the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, and was thoroughly versed in the Chan lineage, the scriptural teaching, and the Pure Land teaching. Even as a child the master was exceptionally intelligent and especially fond of study; among the classics, histories, and the wide range of books there was none he did not examine and read. At the age of twenty-two, through a serious illness he awakened to the impermanence of this illusory body, and immediately resolved to leave the world. After leaving the home life he went about visiting teachers and sitting in their lectures. He went to Xiangjie Temple to hear Master Longyi lecture on the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, and from dawn to dusk he questioned and probed, seeking the profound meaning, until he awakened to the whole purport of that sutra. He then followed Master Hui’an of Zengshou Temple to hear lectures on the Dharma-characteristic school and gained its essential point. Later, sitting at the feet of Master Biankong of Xinhua Temple, he heard the Lotus, the Surangama, the Diamond, and other sutras, and suddenly opened to the perfect understanding, so that the doctrines of the nature school and the appearance school, the one-mind three contemplations, and the meaning of the ten contemplations were entirely free of obstruction. Afterwards he visited Chan Master Cuiruchun of Guangtong Temple to investigate the matter of the supreme vehicle (seeing one’s own nature and realising the mind). Master and disciple answered each other and were wholly in accord, and Master Chun thereupon confirmed him, making him the thirty-sixth patriarch of the Linji school. The master broadly opened his lecture halls, led the assembly in meditation, and exhorted younger students with tireless enthusiasm. For fourteen years, as constant as a single day, his fame spread across the land and the style of his teaching flourished greatly.

But afterwards, whenever Master Chewu recalled Master Yongming — who, though a master of the Chan school, still turned his heart to the Pure Land, reciting the Buddha’s name a hundred thousand times a day and longing for rebirth in the Land of Bliss — he reflected that in the present Dharma-ending age he should all the more follow the legacy of Chan Master Yongming. So he set his mind upon the Pure Land and advocated the Lotus school. Each day he allowed only the time it takes to burn one measure of incense for receiving guests; the rest he devoted entirely to bowing to the Buddha and reciting the Buddha’s name.

The master attained the profound meaning of both the Chan school and the Pure Land school. He was extremely strict with himself and deeply earnest toward others; in his exposition and teaching his words poured forth like water from a vase and gathered like rising clouds, and in his day he was the foremost person of the Dharma-gate. Whenever he set forth the Tathagata’s grace in rescuing beings from suffering and granting them joy, the master would shed tears as he spoke, and none who heard him could keep from weeping until their robes were damp. Master Yongming said:
“One who has Chan and also the Pure Land is like a tiger wearing horns: in this present life he is a teacher of men, and in the life to come he becomes a Buddha and a Patriarch.”
From this one can see the truth of it.

Ten months before his passing, the master already knew the time of his departure. In the second month of the fifteenth year of the Jiaqing era he went to Wanshou Temple to sweep the ancestral pagoda and took leave of the patrons of the mountains. In the third month he returned to the mountain and ordered preparations for his cremation. On the seventeenth day of the tenth month he gathered the assembly, entrusted the affairs of the monastery, and ordered his disciple Songquan to lead the congregation and preside.

[Patrons (wai hu)] the lay people apart from the monks and nuns — such as kinsmen and dana-patrons (almsgivers) — who practise various good deeds for the sake of Buddhism, such as supplying the clergy with clothing and food to support their peaceful cultivation, or doing all they can to protect and advance the spread of the Dharma. [tu pi] cremation.

Half a month before he revealed his passing, he saw in the empty sky countless banners and canopies, coming from the west. He then told the assembly: “The signs of the Pure Land have appeared; I am about to return to the West.” When the assembly urged him to remain in the world by way of exhortation, the master said: “A hundred years are but a sojourn, and in the end there is a place of return.
I have attained the holy state,
and you should rejoice for the master’s sake; why trouble to keep me here?”
[A hundred years are but a sojourn] in living a hundred years, it is nothing more than a temporary lodging. [zhen] to reach; to attain. Example: perfecting it day by day.
On the sixteenth day of the twelfth month he ordered the setting up of the nirvana feast. On the seventeenth day, in the shen period (three in the afternoon), he told the assembly:
“Yesterday I already saw the three great beings Manjusri, Avalokitesvara, and Mahasthamaprapta (Shizhi); now I have again received the Buddha’s personal welcome, and I am now departing.”

The assembly recited the Buddha’s name with ever greater vigour. The master sat upright facing the west, palms joined, and said: “Recite one line of the sacred name and behold one portion of the marks of excellence.” Then he formed the Amitabha mudra with his hands and passed away serenely, and all present smelled a rare fragrance floating in the air. After seven days of offerings his face was as in life, kindly and full, his white hair had turned black, and his complexion was extraordinarily smooth and radiant. After the second seven-day period he was placed in the coffin, and after the third he was cremated, yielding more than a hundred relics.

The master was born in the sixth year of the Qianlong era, on the fourteenth day of the tenth month, in the wei period (one to three in the afternoon), and passed away in the fifteenth year of the Jiaqing era, on the seventeenth day of the twelfth month, in the shen period (three to five in the afternoon). His worldly age was seventy, his monastic age forty-nine, and his Dharma age forty-three. The Collected Works of Master Chewu is widely circulated in the world.
[Monastic age (seng la)] the number of years since a monk or nun received the precepts. [Dharma age (fa la)] the number of years since a bhiksu received the precepts.

The essential way: a single recitation of the Buddha’s name encompasses faith, understanding, cultivation, and realisation; therefore the essentials of the Greater Vehicle, the Lesser Vehicle, and all the sutras are all contained within it. Hence the practice of reciting the name is the essential way.
[Of all gateways of understanding, the essential is to illuminate the mind; of all gateways of practice, the essential is to purify the mind.]
Of all gateways of understanding, the essential is to illumine and realise the true mind; of all gateways of practice, the essential is to remove the defilements of the mind.

[Gateway of understanding (fa men)] the “gateway of the teaching” meant here is the gateway of understanding, that is, what is commonly called the gateway of insight, which chiefly consists in studying and comprehending the doctrine. [Gateway of practice (xing men)] the gateway of practice is to set out upon practice in accordance with the teaching, chiefly devoted to actual cultivation. [Defilements of the mind (xin gou)] another name for the afflictions.

[Since the essential of illuminating the mind is none other than Buddha-recitation. To recollect the Buddha and to recite the Buddha, whether in the present or in the future, one will surely see the Buddha; without relying on any expedient means, the mind naturally opens. Thus — is not Buddha-recitation the essential of illuminating the mind?]

Then, for illuminating and realising the true mind there is nothing more excellent than Buddha-recitation. For in recollecting the Buddha and reciting the Buddha, whether in the present or in the future, one will certainly see the Buddha; without borrowing any other expedient means (without reliance on expedient means) the true mind is fully revealed (the mind naturally opens — this is the state of great and complete awakening). This being so, is not Buddha-recitation the essential of illuminating the mind?

[Moreover, the essential of purifying the mind is likewise none other than Buddha-recitation. When a single thought accords, that thought is Buddha; when every thought accords, every thought is Buddha. When a clear jewel is cast into murky water, the murky water cannot but become clear; when the Buddha’s name is cast into a confused mind, the confused mind cannot but become Buddha. Thus — is not Buddha-recitation the essential of purifying the mind?]

Furthermore, for purifying the defilements of the mind there is nothing more excellent than Buddha-recitation. When a single thought accords, that thought is Buddha (and that thought, of course, is free of affliction); when every thought accords, every thought is Buddha. When a clear jewel is cast into murky water, the murky water cannot but grow clear; when the Buddha’s name is cast into a vexed and scattered mind, that vexed and scattered mind cannot but turn into the serene, bright, and still Buddha-mind. This being so, is not Buddha-recitation the essential of purifying the mind?

[When a single thought accords, that thought is Buddha; when every thought accords, every thought is Buddha] when the pure and unmixed thought of Buddha-recitation is present (no deluded thought being mingled within this single line of the name), it is called “a single thought of accord.” “Accord” bears the meaning “this very mind is making the Buddha; this very mind is the Buddha.” (See the section on
“a Single Thought of Accord”
below.) [Clear jewel] a precious jewel that can purify murky water. The “Three Periods of Recollection” of Zhongfeng says:

“In the Western region there is a precious thing called the clear jewel. It is said that when this jewel is thrown into murky water, if it enters an inch of the water, that inch of murky water becomes clear immediately. As the jewel enters the water, from an inch to a foot and even to the bottom, the murky water likewise follows it and becomes clear and still. Know then that the clear jewel is a metaphor for the pure thought of Buddha-recitation; the murky water is a metaphor for the confused and scattered deluded mind.”

[A single recitation of the Buddha’s name encompasses the essentials of both the gateway of awakening and the gateway of cultivation. When awakening is raised, faith is within it; when cultivation is raised, realisation is within it. Faith, understanding, cultivation, and realisation are all encompassed, and the essentials of the greater and lesser vehicles and of all the sutras are exhausted without remainder. Then — is not this single Amitabha the essential way?]

From the above one can see that a single recitation of the Buddha’s name encompasses the essentials of both the gateway of awakening and the gateway of cultivation. When awakening is spoken of, faith is within it; when cultivation is spoken of, realisation is within it. A single recitation of the Buddha’s name encompasses faith, understanding, cultivation, and realisation, so that the essentials of the Greater Vehicle, the Lesser Vehicle, and all the sutras are entirely contained within this single name. Then — is not this single Amitabha Buddha the essential way?
[qing wu bu jin] here means contained without omission. “Qing” means to use up, all of it.

The conditions of rebirth: each thought we give rise to becomes a condition for rebirth in a future life. Carefully examine the thoughts that arise in the course of daily life — with which of the ten dharma-realms they accord most, and with which they accord most intensely — and then, without asking anyone else, you will know clearly which realm you will be reborn into in the next life and what your circumstances will be.

[This present thought of ours is, in its entirety, the true turned into delusion, and, in its entirety, the delusion that is itself the true; through the day it is unchanging, and through the day it follows conditions. If one does not follow the conditions of the Buddha-realm to think of the Buddha-realm, then one thinks of the nine realms; if one does not think of the three vehicles, then one thinks of the six ordinary realms; if one does not think of humans and devas, then one thinks of the three evil paths; if one does not think of ghosts and animals, then one thinks of hell. For as long as there is a mind, there cannot be no thought. And the mind-substance of no-thought is realised by the Buddha alone. From the stage of equal enlightenment downward, all beings have thought. Whatever thought arises must fall within the ten realms; there is no thought that goes beyond the ten realms, because the ten dharma-realms have no outside.]

This present thought of ours is either the deluded mind or the true mind; the substance of the mind is unchanging through the day, yet its state of delusion or awakening changes through the day as it follows the objects and thoughts it relies upon. If one does not follow the conditions of the Buddha-dharma-realm to think of the Buddha-dharma-realm, then one conditions the other nine dharma-realms and thinks of them. Within these nine realms, if one does not condition the three vehicles (sravaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva), then one conditions the six ordinary realms (hell, hungry ghost, animal, asura, human, deva). Within the six ordinary realms, if one does not condition humans and devas, then one conditions the three evil paths (hell, hungry ghost, animal). Within the three evil paths, if one does not condition ghosts and animals, then one conditions hell. This is all because, so long as there is a mind, one cannot be without thought. For the mind-substance of complete no-thought is realised by the Buddha alone; from the bodhisattva at the stage of equal enlightenment downward, all beings have thought. Then, whatever thought arises must be a thought of one of the ten realms, because the ten dharma-realms already encompass everything.

[The whole true becomes delusion; the whole delusion is itself the true] this present thought of the mind has two states, the true and the deluded. When self-nature holds sway it is true; when habitual tendencies hold sway it is deluded. “The whole true becomes delusion, the whole delusion is itself the true” means that true and deluded do not stand side by side; either it is wholly true or wholly deluded. In a single thought of delusion, the whole true mind becomes a deluded mind (the whole true becomes delusion); in a single thought of awakening, the whole deluded mind becomes a true mind (the whole delusion is itself the true). The “true” here means the original — that is, the true mind is the original state of the mind; the “deluded” means deluded movement, that which is confused. Because the original state is muddied and confused by deluded movement, the true mind becomes the deluded mind. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “In the previous thought of delusion, one is an ordinary person; in the later thought of awakening, one is a Buddha.” [Unchanging through the day, following conditions through the day] although the mind has the distinction of delusion and awakening — in delusion the whole true becomes delusion, in awakening the whole delusion is itself the true — yet the substance of the mind (self-nature) is in no way altered (without arising, ceasing, increase, or decrease), as it is said: “Unchanging through the day, following conditions through the day; following conditions through the day, unchanging through the day.” [The ten dharma-realms] hell, hungry ghost, animal, asura, human, deva, sravaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, Buddha. The first six are the six ordinary realms; the last four are the four sages. [Bodhisattva of equal enlightenment] among the fifty-two stages of the Greater Vehicle, the fifty-first stage is called equal enlightenment; this is the bodhisattva about to realise Buddhahood, whose merit and wisdom are nearly equal to the Buddha’s, hence the name “equal enlightenment.” The fifty-second stage is Buddhahood.
[Each thought one gives rise to is a condition for rebirth. If one truly understands this principle and yet does not recite the Buddha’s name — there has never been such a one.]
Each thought we give rise to becomes a condition for rebirth in a future life. If one truly understands this principle and yet does not recite the Buddha’s name, such a person can never exist.

[If this mind can accord with equanimity, great compassion, the merits of the proper and dependent rewards, and the sublime name of myriad virtues, then it is thinking of the Buddha-realm. If it can accord with the bodhi-mind, the six perfections, and the myriad practices, then it is thinking of the bodhisattva-realm. With a mind of non-self, according with the twelve links of dependent origination, it is thinking of the pratyekabuddha-realm. With a mind of non-self, contemplating the four noble truths, it is thinking of the sravaka-realm.]

If this present thought accords with the Buddha’s equanimity, great compassion, the merits of the proper and dependent rewards, and the sublime name of myriad virtues, then it is thinking of the Buddha-realm; if it accords with the bodhi-mind, the six perfections, and the myriad practices, then it is thinking of the bodhisattva-realm; with a mind of non-self, according with the twelve links of dependent origination, it is thinking of the pratyekabuddha-realm; with a mind of non-self, contemplating the four noble truths, it is thinking of the sravaka-realm.

[Proper and dependent rewards (yi zheng)] the dependent reward and the proper reward. The lands, dwellings, houses, and implements of the world are that upon which the body relies, and are called the “dependent reward”; the body of a sentient being, formed by the temporary union of the five aggregates, is the result of karma created in past lives, and is called the “proper reward.”

[If it accords with the four dhyanas and the eight concentrations, as well as the highest grade of the ten wholesome deeds, then it is thinking of the deva-realm. If it accords with the five precepts, then it is thinking of the human realm. If one cultivates the precepts, wholesome deeds, and other such dharmas while harbouring a mind of hatred, pride, and victory, then one falls into the asura-realm.]

If this present thought accords with the four dhyanas and the eight concentrations, as well as the supreme ten wholesome deeds, then it is thinking of the deva-realm; if it accords with the five precepts, then it is thinking of the human realm; if one cultivates the precepts, the ten wholesome deeds, and other such dharmas while harbouring a mind of resentment, pride, and competition, then it is thinking of the asura-realm.

[The four dhyanas and eight concentrations] the four dhyanas are the four concentrations of the form realm; the eight concentrations are the four dhyanas of the form realm and the four formless concentrations of the formless realm. [The ten wholesome deeds] the ten kinds of wholesome karma: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, not speaking divisively, not speaking harshly, not speaking idly, not being greedy, not being hateful, not being deluded. [The five precepts] not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, not drinking alcohol. Not killing is not taking the life of living creatures; not stealing is not taking the property of others; not committing sexual misconduct is not engaging in sexual acts outside the bond of marriage; not speaking falsely is not uttering deceitful and fraudulent words; not drinking alcohol is not consuming intoxicating drinks or drugs.
[If, with a gentle
(identical with “soft”)

mind, one thinks of the lower grade of the ten evil deeds, then one falls into the animal-realm. Or, with a mind at once relaxed and intense, according with the middle grade of the ten evil deeds, one falls into the hungry-ghost realm. If, with a fierce and blazing mind, one accords with the highest grade of the ten evil deeds, then one falls into the hell-realm. The ten evil deeds are killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, idle speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, greed, hatred, and wrong views; to do the opposite of these is the ten wholesome deeds.]

If, with a gentle (not intense) mind, one thinks of the milder ten evil deeds, then one is thinking of the animal-realm. If, with a somewhat intense mind, one accords with the middling ten evil deeds, then one is thinking of the hungry-ghost realm. If, with a very intense (fierce and blazing) mind, one accords with the worst of the ten evil deeds, then one is thinking of the hell-realm. The ten evil deeds are killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, idle speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, greed, hatred, and ignorance; to do the opposite of these is the ten wholesome deeds.

[One should closely examine the thoughts that arise in daily life — with which realm they accord most, and with which they accord most intensely — and then the place where one will settle one’s body and establish one’s destiny in a future life, without troubling to ask another.]

One should carefully examine the thoughts that arise in the course of daily life — with which of the ten dharma-realms they accord most, and with which they accord most intensely — and then, without asking anyone else, you will know clearly which realm you will be reborn into in the next life and what your circumstances (the place where you will settle) will be.
[mi] fine and detailed; minute.

Carefully examine the thoughts that arise in the course of daily life — with which of the ten dharma-realms they accord most, and with which they accord most intensely — this is the very place of self-examination! Therefore the effort of cultivation must be made where thoughts arise.

blocks.text: 3. Karmic Retribution Manifested in the Mind

inline.s: Karmic retribution manifested in the mind: all states are produced by karma and manifested by the mind. The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is produced by pure karma and manifested by a pure mind. Therefore a cultivator who with single-minded focus recites the Buddha’s name and diligently cultivates pure karma will surely, through karmic response, be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[All states are produced by karma and manifested by the mind. In the very place where they appear, their own substance is the mind. As long as there is a mind, there cannot be a state absent. If the Buddha-state does not appear, then the states of the nine realms appear. If the states of the three vehicles do not appear, then the states of the six ordinary realms appear. If the states of devas, humans, ghosts, and animals do not appear, then the states of hell appear.]

All states are produced by karma and manifested by the mind. And the state that appears is itself the self-mind. As long as there is a mind, there cannot be a state absent. If this mind does not manifest the Buddha-state, it manifests the states of the nine realms (hell, hungry ghost, animal, asura, human, deva, sravaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva). If it does not manifest the states of the three vehicles (the Sravaka Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, the Bodhisattva Vehicle), it manifests the states of the six ordinary realms (that is, the six paths, for the six paths are all ordinary beings, hence the name “six ordinary realms”). If it does not manifest the states of devas, humans, ghosts, and animals, it manifests the states of hell.

[The states manifested by the Buddha and the three vehicles, though differing in their degree of superiority, are all, in essentials, enjoyment of the bliss of Dharma. The states manifested by the devas of the three realms are solely the enjoyment of the bliss of concentration and of the five objects of desire. The state of the human path is mixed with suffering and joy, each following its own karma, in varying measure. The states of ghosts and animals have much suffering and little joy. As for hell, it is wholly and solely extreme suffering.]

The states manifested by the minds of the Buddha and the three vehicles, though differing in excellence and inferiority, are all, in the essential thing, the enjoyment of the bliss of Dharma. The states manifested by the minds of the devas of the three realms are all the enjoyment of the bliss of concentration and of the five objects of desire. The state manifested by the mind of the human path has both suffering and joy, each person following his own karmic retribution, the proportion of suffering and joy differing. The states manifested by the minds of hungry ghosts and animals have much suffering and little joy. As for the state manifested by the mind of hell, it is wholly and solely extreme suffering.

[The three realms] the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. [The five objects of desire] form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Form refers to beautiful appearances; sound to melodious tones; smell to fragrant scents; taste to delicious flavours; touch to agreeable sensations. Because these five can cause one to give rise to a mind of greed and desire, they are called the five objects of desire.

[As the mountains, rivers, people, and things seen in a dream are all manifested by the dream-mind. Without the dream-mind there would certainly be no dream-state. And if there were no dream-state, neither would there be a dream-mind. Therefore know: apart from the mind there is no state, and apart from the state there is no mind. The whole state is the mind, and the whole mind is the state. If one would investigate the fruit within the cause, one should contemplate the mind; if one would verify the cause at the place of the fruit, one should contemplate the state. Hence it is said there has never been a state without a mind, and never a mind without a state. The fruit must follow from the cause, and the cause must realise the fruit. If one truly knows this principle that mind and state, cause and fruit, are one and not two, and yet still does not recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land — I do not believe it.]

This is like the mountains, rivers, people, and things one sees in a dream, all manifested by the dream-mind. If there were no dream-mind, there would certainly be no dream-state. Suppose there were no dream-state; then there would also be no dream-mind. Therefore we know: apart from the mind there is no state, and apart from the state there is no mind. The state is the mind, and the mind is the state. If one would investigate (come to know) the fruit within the cause, one must contemplate the mind; if one would verify (examine) the cause at the place of the fruit, one must contemplate the state. Therefore it is said: there is no state without a mind, and no mind without a state. The fruit must come from the cause, and the cause must manifest the fruit. If one truly knows this principle of mind and state, cause and fruit, as one and not two, and yet still does not recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss — I cannot believe it!
[yi ru, one suchness] not two and not different — this is called one suchness.

blocks.text: 4. The Essential Doctrine of the Pure Land

inline.s: The essential doctrine of the Pure Land: to take birth and death as a matter of genuine concern, to awaken the bodhi-mind, and, with deep faith and vows, to hold fast to the Buddha’s name.
[gang zong, essential doctrine] the principal outline and central purport.

[The sixteen words — “to take birth and death as a matter of genuine concern, to awaken the bodhi-mind, and, with deep faith and vows, to hold fast to the Buddha’s name” — are the one great essential doctrine of the gateway of Buddha-recitation.]

To take birth and death as a matter of genuine concern, to awaken the bodhi-mind, and, with deep faith and vows, to hold fast to the Buddha’s name” — these sixteen words are the one great essential doctrine of the gateway of Buddha-recitation.

[If the mind of “taking birth and death as a matter of genuine concern” is not aroused, then all instruction is nothing but idle words. Of all the heavy suffering in the world, none exceeds birth and death. If birth and death is not ended, then there is death upon death, birth upon birth, there being death in birth and birth in death. Out of one womb, into another womb; casting off one skin-bag, taking up another skin-bag — the suffering is already unbearable. Moreover, since the round of rebirth is not yet escaped, falling is unavoidable. The womb of a pig, the womb of a dog — into which will one not bore? The skin-bag of a donkey, the skin-bag of a horse — which will one not take up?]

If a cultivator does not arouse the mind of genuinely seeking to escape birth and death, then all instruction is, for him, merely idle talk (frivolous words). Of all the greatest suffering in the world, none exceeds birth and death. If birth and death is not ended, then there is birth upon birth and death upon death, the wheel of rebirth turning without cease. Out of one womb (dying), into another womb (being reborn); casting off one foul skin-bag (dying), taking up another foul skin-bag (being reborn) — the suffering is beyond words. Moreover, since the round of rebirth is not yet escaped, falling into the three evil paths is unavoidable. The womb of a pig, the womb of a dog — into which will one not bore? The skin-bag of a donkey, the skin-bag of a horse — which will one not take up?
[xi lun, idle words] words that have a playful and unrealistic character.

[This human body is the most difficult to obtain and the most easily lost. Through a single thought’s error one falls into an evil realm. The three evil paths are easy to enter and difficult to leave; the duration in hell is long and its suffering heavy. Whereas the seven Buddhas came and went, it has still been an ant; after eighty thousand kalpas, it has not escaped the body of a dove. The duration in the animal path is already extreme, and the duration in the ghost and hell paths is many times longer. Long enduring through endless kalpas — when is there an end, when a resting place? Amid the agonies of ten thousand sufferings, there is no refuge and no rescue. At every utterance of this, the hairs of the body stand on end. Each time one thinks of it, the five viscera burn as with fire. Therefore, from this very moment, one should acutely grieve over birth and death, as in mourning one’s father and mother, with the urgency of putting out a fire blazing on one’s head
(an archaic form of “burn”)

This human body is the most difficult to obtain and yet the most easily lost. Through a single thought’s error one enters an evil path. The three evil paths are easy to enter and hard to leave; if one falls into the hell path, the time is long and the suffering heavy. If one falls into the animal path, being deluded and attached to its body, life after life it is still that same animal. For example, a nest of ants — since the time of the seven Buddhas they have always been ants; and the dove, after eighty thousand kalpas, is still a dove. The time in the animal path is already extremely long, while the time in the hungry-ghost and hell paths is several times longer still. Long enduring through endless kalpas — when is there an end? Amid the agonies of ten thousand sufferings, there is neither refuge nor rescue. These circumstances, at every word of them, make the hairs of the body stand on end. Each time one thinks of them, the five viscera burn as if on fire. Therefore from this very moment one must grieve acutely over birth and death, as one mourns the death of one’s father and mother, with the urgency of one putting out a fire blazing on his head.

[Since the seven Buddhas, it has still been an ant] animals are deluded and always attached to this very physical body, and so their time in the animal path is extremely long. When the Jetavana Vihara was being built and the wall was being dug, the Buddha saw a nest of ants and said to the elder Sudatta: these ants have, since the time of the seven Buddhas, always been ants. [The seven Buddhas] the seven Buddhas of the past, namely Vipasyin Buddha, Sikhin Buddha, Visvabhu Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kashyapa Buddha, and Shakyamuni Buddha. [After eighty thousand kalpas, it has not escaped the body of a dove] one day the Buddha saw a dove and at once said to his disciples: this dove, even after eighty thousand kalpas, will still be a dove. [As in mourning one’s father and mother] grief as when one’s parents have died. [kao, bi] (deceased) father and mother.

[And yet I have birth and death, and I seek to escape. And all sentient beings are in birth and death, and all of them should escape. They and I are originally of one body. They are all my parents from many lives past, and Buddhas of the future. If one does not think of saving them all but seeks only one’s own benefit, then there is a deficiency in principle and the heart is not at ease. Moreover, if the great mind is not aroused, then outwardly one cannot be in communion with the Buddhas, and inwardly one cannot accord with one’s own nature; above, one cannot perfectly accomplish the Buddha Way, and below, one cannot broadly benefit the multitude of beings. The beginningless bonds of love — how can they be released? The beginningless debts of grievance — how can they be resolved? The karmic offences accumulated over many kalpas are hard to repent of; the roots of goodness accumulated over many kalpas are hard to bring to maturity. Whatever one cultivates is beset by many obstacles. Even should there be some accomplishment, in the end it falls into the one-sided and small. Therefore one must, in accord with one’s nature, awaken the great bodhi-mind.]

And yet I have birth and death, and I seek to escape. And all sentient beings are in birth and death, and all of them should escape. They and I are originally of one body; they are all my parents from many lives past, and also Buddhas of the future. If I do not save them all but seek only my own liberation, then there is a deficiency in principle and my heart is not at ease. Moreover, if the great mind (the bodhi-mind) is not aroused, then outwardly one cannot be in communion with the Buddhas, and inwardly one cannot accord with one’s own nature; above, one cannot perfectly accomplish the Buddha Way, and below, one cannot broadly benefit the multitude of beings. This being so, the beginningless bonds of love — how can they be released? The beginningless debts of grievance — how can they be resolved? The karmic offences accumulated over countless kalpas are difficult to repent of; the roots of goodness accumulated over countless kalpas are difficult to bring to maturity. Cultivating in this way, one is confronted at all times and places with many obstacles serving as tigers in one’s path. Even should there be some accomplishment, in the end it is an incomplete (one-sided) small fruit. Therefore one must, in accord with one’s nature, awaken the great bodhi-mind!

[Awaken the bodhi-mind] to arouse the great mind of seeking the Buddha Way above (to attain Buddhahood) and saving sentient beings below. Master Xing’an, in his “Exhortation to Awaken the Bodhi-Mind,” says: “The essential gateway to entering the Way is to make the resolve foremost; the urgent task of cultivation is to establish the vow first. When the vow is established, sentient beings can be saved; when the resolve is aroused, the Buddha Way can be accomplished. If one does not arouse the vast mind and establish the firm vow, then even should one pass through kalpas of dust, one would still remain in the round of rebirth; though one may cultivate, it is all in vain and full of toil. Therefore the Avatamsaka Sutra says: ‘To forget the bodhi-mind while practising all good dharmas is called the work of Mara.’ Forgetting it is already thus; how much more so never having aroused it? Hence one knows that if one wishes to learn the Tathagata Vehicle, one must first fully arouse the bodhisattva’s vow; this cannot be delayed.” [The Tathagata Vehicle] the teaching that leads beings to Buddhahood. A vehicle is a conveyance, used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s teaching; the teaching can carry beings to the far shore of nirvana, and so it is called a “vehicle.”

[Since the great mind has been aroused, one should cultivate the great practice. And among all the gateways of practice, to seek the one most easy to begin, most easy to accomplish, most perfectly stable, and most perfectly sudden and complete — there is none like “with deep faith and vows, to hold fast to the Buddha’s name.”]

Since the great mind has been aroused, one should cultivate the great practice. And among all the gateways of practice, seeking the one most easy to begin, most easy to accomplish, and again most perfectly stable and most perfectly sudden and complete — there is nothing surpassing “with deep faith and vows, to hold fast to the Buddha’s name.”

Master Xing’an, in a verse instructing a meditator on Buddha-recitation, said: “One line of Amitabha is a case in point. No further deliberation is needed; settle it on the spot at once. Like a great fire, touch it and it burns. Like the sword Tai’a, oppose it and it is destroyed. The eighty-four thousand treasure-hoards of Dharma are wholly gathered in six words. The seventeen hundred tangled vines (the seventeen hundred cases of the Chan tradition) are cut through with a single stroke (with one line of the Buddha’s name, the tangled vines are all severed). Let the Buddha not be fond of hearing them; I for my part recall and recite with mind and heart. Pray do not speak many words; only keep the single mind unconfused.” (From the Records of Pure Land Sages)
